So I bought Stardew Valley thinking I'd relax for an hour.
That was January 2026.
I have no idea what year it is anymore.
The game starts innocently enough. You inherit a charming little farm, meet friendly townsfolk, pet some chickens, and think, "I'll just water my crops and then go to bed."
That, my friends,  was the first lie.
Every in-game day ends with:
"Okay, just one more day."
Then suddenly you're optimizing sprinkler layouts like you're managing a Fortune 500 company. You're carrying seventeen different crops, twelve jars of mayonnaise, three mysterious artifacts, a fish that only appears every third Tuesday during a thunderstorm at exactly 6:40 PM while Mercury is in retrograde, and somehow you're still late to Pierre's before he closes.
Meanwhile, real life has completely fallen apart.
My laundry has become an archaeological dig site.
My dishes have formed diplomati
Love this game, but please remember to go to bed before 2 either in the game or in real life.

Cant believe Stardew Valley is already 10 years old fr.
600mb+ is such a small file size, just a few mins to download. But at the same time, its also huge enough to contain the life Ive always dreamed of.
I was promised a relaxing game, instead, it made me learn Excel formulas and obsess over my farm like it's an actual job. And the worst part - I've enjoyed that.
Its like crack but cheaper and with good music. 10/10 would recommend and also Leah is a baddie

Initially, I wasn't interested in playing it. My friends highly recommended it and basically forced me to give it a try. The result? I am completely hooked. It really reminds me of Harvest Moon: Back to Nature, giving me a great sense of nostalgia. On top of that, the game doesn't just focus on farming. You can actually go on adventures and fight monsters in the mines and other areas.

​I also enjoy the plot twists included in the game. The NPCs actually go about their daily routines, which makes the world feel incredibly alive. I love that you get to choose between restoring the Community Center or buying a JojaMart membership, since this choice actually impacts the storyline.

​Overall, I absolutely love this game. I really hope they release a sequel someday with fresh plot twists, along with new monsters and crops to discover🤍

I've been playing Stardew Valley for years, and recently came back to it again. Despite having hundreds of hours, I still haven't achieved all that much, and honestly, I think that's part of why I love it. Over the past few years, my mental and physical health have deteriorated a lot. I spend most of my days inside and often feel overwhelmed, exhausted, and lacking the energy or motivation to do much of anything.
I've stopped playing many of the bigger games I used to love because I feel too much pressure to perform or finish them. But Stardew is different. There's nothing I have to do. I can just play at my own pace. I recently started a new save, and all I'm doing is planting and harvesting crops. For a few hours every night, I zone out, farm, and listen to a podcast. [h2] The gold Standard of Cozy Gaming [/h2] 
​It is genuinely mind-blowing to think that Stardew Valley was created by just one person. When you compare it to other titles—which I won't name—that stay stuck in Early Access for years despite having entire studios behind them, Eric Barone’s achievement is even more impressive. This isn't just a farming sim; it is a labor of love that has become the definitive blueprint for what a "cozy game" should be.

​The beauty of Stardew is that the pacing is entirely up to you. You can play it as a chill, relaxing escape where you just enjoy the scenery, or you can go full "hard-grind" mode and try to complete the Community Center challenge in a single year. Whether you want to min-max your profits or just spend your days fishing, the game never forces a specific playstyle on you. With the variety of seasons, festivals, unique crops, and hidden se

Stardew Valley is a very relaxing and therapeutic game. In it, you play as a farmer, primarily farming, fishing, raising animals, and gathering resources. You work from sunrise to sunset, without modern high-tech drones or automated farms; everything is primitive and simple, just like its pixelated art style.

Through countless days and nights in the game, I built friendships and even love with the townspeople. I respect and cherish every NPC in the game, talking to them, listening to their dreams and secrets, just as if they were my friends in real life.

Stardew Valley is honestly overrated. Don’t get me wrong, it’s not a bad game at all, but it’s incredibly shallow. Once you finish it once, there’s really no strong reason to keep going. The loop starts repeating itself and there’s not much depth beyond the first full playthrough. I have more hours than I normally would because it’s one of the few games my girlfriend plays, so we spent some time on it together — otherwise I probably would’ve dropped it much earlier.

If you’re not a fan of slow-paced gameplay, this probably won’t be for you. I’ve watched videos about how challenging the development process was, and I have a lot of respect for the effort that went into it—and for Eric Barone’s well-deserved success.

That said, it ultimately comes down to personal preference, and the gameplay style just isn’t for me.

JUst a calming, relaxing experience, y'know. You can go at your own pace, as long as the game doesn't decide to just say no to everything you want to do on any given day.

This is my first life sim game I've played, and perhaps some of my critique is applicable to this genre as a whole. 
I'll start off by saying this game has insane quality of life issues (mainly NPC related). I haven't in my life played a game that needed that many QoL mods like this one. I would never play this game unmodded. 
A lot of the gameplay is just walking from place to place, doing chores, and you could argue that this is what life sim games are about, but what's the point if it's not fun?

It's the type of game I'd play while binge-watching House M.D., and it's definitely not entertaining enough on its own.
probably just not my style of game, but i found it overwhelming and kind of unsatisfyingly grindy.

Looking for a soothing cure for my PTSD, I found this game surprising and fun, but stressful instead of soothing.

This game should be one of the tests for ADHD because it feels like a personal hell for a person with ADHD

While playing I would have waves of enjoyment and boredom. I would do everything i could do, and then like an in-game week later will unlock a new thing that opens up the world a whole lot more. This game has overtaken my life. I don't think about climbing the corporate ladder anymore. I only want to farm. The years of study for my degree, now worthless. I quit the corporate lifestyle for a different kind of grind. I eat, sleep and breath this game. It's all consuming.

The gameplay is fairly monotonous, and the NPCs have very sterile interactions.
It's a grind, no skill is required anywhere, mechanics simply boil down to get money by clicking left mouse until you run out of energy for the day, so you are then forced to forage or 'interact' with the townsfolk.
Nothing is random, all NPC activity and game elements are on rails.
In all honesty, this is the game that made me realize I don't like cozy games.
The artwork is pretty good, except for some color choices (yellow dirt?!). Music is pretty good, and compliments the game well.

​Stardew Valley is, at its core, a masterpiece of the cozy-farming genre. Whether you’re meticulously planning your crop rotations, delving into the mines, or wooing the local villagers, the game offers a level of charm and depth that is rarely matched. It shines brightest when played with a partner or friends—sharing the workload of a growing farm makes the experience feel truly collaborative and rewarding.
​The Breaking Point: "Connecting to Online Services..."
